newsitem.title: UK: OCUS-Gold, commodities don't benefit from Wall St.
newsitem.headline: OCUS-Gold, commodities don't benefit from Wall St.

text.p: Dark clouds over Wall Street failed to send investors running for shelter in the gold market, where prices finished slightly weaker on Monday.
The weakness in equities also failed to attract money to other commodity markets, analysts said.
Investors, rattled by gold's decline to 12-year lows this year, have shunned the former "safe haven" despite a 250-point plunge on the U.S. stock market last Friday.
"They are very wary of gold. It's been a dreadful investment," said analyst Ted Arnold of Merrill Lynch.
"If they are worried about the stock market falling and want a safe haven, they'll go in to cash for a time and then maybe bonds, but it's not going be gold."
Even worse for gold bugs, underhedged producers are increasingly worried about locking in profits and have taken to selling into any small rally.
Gold closed at $323.25 an ounce in London, down $1.10 from Friday's closing level.
Prices slid from early highs above $326.00 an ounce as investors skipped out of the market, disappointed by gold's unimpressive price performance on Friday.
A modest recovery by Wall Street and the dollar's revival on Monday also prompted buyers to stay away.
Recurring fears about the prospect of central banks selling some more of their gold reserves have also dampened enthusiasm, as have fears of a U.S. interest rate rise in future.
"If we do get a rate rise you'll see gold down on producer selling rather than see it climb on the back of a stock exchange fall," one dealer said.
In other commodities, base metals were down sharply, following on losses from last Friday.
Several traders said equities markets were not the main spark for the losses seen in the industrial metals.
But analysts said that the aggressive selling on Friday was probably linked to the stock market.

"The sharp fall in the Dow showed the economy is weakening which is not good for metals, especially copper. As the stock market crashed investors sold bonds or commodities to pay for losses," analyst Robin Bhar of brokers Brandeis said.

Copper for three month delivery on the London Metal Exchange (LME) sank to near seven-month lows, finishing the afternoon kerb at $2,162 per tonne -- a loss of more than $100, or around six percent, since last Thursday.
Copper had been looking vulnerable in recent weeks as supplies became more available. LME stocks have more than doubled this year to 260,875 tonnes, with the bulk of the rise seen in July.
On Monday, aluminium and zinc got caught up in copper's slipstream, also seeing losses.
The soft commodities were seasonally quiet and failed to show much immediate reaction to Wall Street.
Cocoa drifted higher while coffee was easier following slightly bearish U.S. coffee stocks data.
Sugar pared gains posted in a strong rally on Friday which traders attributed to the move to chart-based fund buying rather than a direct link to the stock market.
Crude oil futures were easier after coming under pressure from views in the market that U.S. gasoline demand was weakening at the end of the summer holiday season.
